toc.title: Shutdown needs to be experienced mindfully

blocks.p: Someone left a comment on one of my YouTube videos asking, "Is it possible to come out of polyvagal shutdown?"

Of course, the answer is generally yes. But I think it's important to keep coming back to the basics of the Polyvagal Theory, to make sure we're grounded in what we understand about it, and then see how it applies to questions like this one: coming out of shutdown, or climbing our polyvagal ladder.

The first thing we want to do is understand what we mean by shutdown. Shutdown is a state of the autonomic nervous system. It's the bottom of the polyvagal ladder. It's the last autonomic shift that would happen in the face of a life threat.

Say we're in a situation where we can't use socialization to deal with it, we can't run away from it, and we can't fight it off. The last option our autonomic nervous system has is pretty much to either freeze or shut down. We're focusing on shutdown here. To shut down is to collapse: a death feign, or a faint, to appear dead. And that can actually increase the chances of survival.

When we're in shutdown, our body is basically playing dead. It's conserving resources in case we have the opportunity to come out of shutdown, up the polyvagal ladder, into fight. It's there because it serves an evolutionary function. It's a biological response, and I think it's really important to keep reminding ourselves of that.

I mentioned freeze. Shutdown is different from freeze. Freeze is more of a tense stiffening. It's a paralyzed kind of look, an immobilization, but with tension: immobilized while in flight or fight. Freeze does involve shutdown, but it's a mixed state. It's shutdown plus flight or fight.
Shutdown is a primary state all by itself. It's simply that limp collapse. It can also involve dissociation and numbing. The entire body is shutting down, disconnecting from reality, going numb.

That serves the organism in that situation, so it doesn't have to feel pain. It also serves the organism for coming out of it. If it's conserved its resources, then when it comes up into fight and flight, it has what it needs to mobilize: a sympathetic surge to use aggression, then evasion, and then, hopefully, to get to safety.
So, is it possible to come out of shutdown? Yes, it's definitely possible. I see it in therapy pretty darn often.

All of these polyvagal states evolved within us as a way to optimize bodily resources, in the face of danger, life threat, or even safety. In the safety state, it's about optimizing for health, growth, and restoration. In flight and fight, it's about mobilization. And in shutdown, it's about conserving resources.

What I want you to take from that is that it's a biological response. We shift into that state as a response to something. And we can shift out of it, partially, once the danger or life threat is gone. But we can also shift out of it as a response to safety.
I want you to look at this in a couple of different ways.

One is shutdown as a functional response in the face of a life threat. It's possible to come out of that, up into fight, then flight, and then into safety. That would be an intense situation where someone is actually in danger. It's not a stuck state.

That's the difference between a stuck state and a non-stuck state. A wild animal can go into a shutdown response and not get stuck. That mammal drops to the bottom of its polyvagal ladder, but it's not stuck there. It can come out when there's an opportunity to do so.
That's different from a human who gets stuck in shutdown. For us, part of it is: is there an absence of life threat that allows us to come out of shutdown? But also:

ul: Is there the presence of literal safety, in the environment?
Is there literal safety with other people, safe connections, co-regulation?
And is the person who is stuck in shutdown able to listen to that shutdown state and be with it mindfully?

blocks.p: If they can mindfully be with it, they can allow it to complete and come out of shutdown. They feel the impulse to be in shutdown, and then they also feel the impulse to come out of it and up into fight.
So what is needed to come out of shutdown? Typically, someone in shutdown needs to slowly allow the sympathetic flight and fight energy to return, and it's going to be fight first.

Deb Dana described that path when I interviewed her: "To begin to leave dorsal, you have to travel through sympathetic… we have to have our energy used in an organized way and often in connection with somebody else." ([Episode 29](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c))

To get there, the person needs to listen to the needs of their shutdown state. All of the polyvagal states have impulses that stem from them. They look different from individual to individual, but each basic state has impulses that come with it. If you can listen to those impulses and mindfully act on them, then climbing the polyvagal ladder is going to happen.
For somebody in shutdown, the impulses typically look something like this:

ul: Predictability. Spontaneity is not going to be a great thing for someone who is more in shutdown.
Soothing music, or no music at all.

blocks.p: That's what it can generally look like, but each person needs to listen to their specific body and what it needs, and to what shutdown feels like for them.

In therapy, it usually sounds something like this: "I feel the need to just go to bed, be under my covers, in the fetal position, in the dark." There's an impulse to hide. There's an impulse to be alone. There's an impulse to immobilize with low stimulation. Your own version might be slightly different. I've had someone say they wanted to do basically the same thing, but inside their closet. That was their safe space.

What often happens is that someone feels an impulse like this in their shutdown state, but doesn't actually listen to it mindfully and allow it to be there. They don't allow the shutdown feelings to be there, and they don't allow that impulse to be alone, in mindfulness, to happen.

Instead, they stay in the room endlessly, and instead of feeling what they have to feel, they try to keep their mind off it. Swiping through their phone endlessly. Seeking out entertainment, watching TV, playing video games. Closing the door and blocking people out. They might be in the darkness, but they're not really experiencing it. They're looking for distraction from their emptiness rather than actually feeling it: what it's like to be in shutdown, and to feel some of that emptiness inside of them.

blocks.h: Shutdown needs to be experienced mindfully

blocks.p: Shutdown, just like the other polyvagal states, really needs to be experienced mindfully. That means that on some level, you actually welcome it, or allow it to be there.

That might sound extremely difficult, and yes, it is. Typically it's not something you can just jump into, unless you already have some kind of mindfulness practice within you. So there's an order to it:

ol: Learn the Polyvagal Theory. You actually have to learn this foundational knowledge.
Build your safety state. Once you have that down, work on your capacity to feel safety in your system, so you can anchor yourself in safety.

Feel into your defensive states. Once that's done, then it's time to start feeling into your stuck defensive states, like feeling into shutdown: feeling your defensive state without it being overwhelming, keeping access to your safety state, and mindfully allowing the experience of your stuck shutdown, or flight and fight, or freeze.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.
